i need help with my one-page appeal memo for HR
they’re cutting my base pay 12% because i moved to boise

payroll freeze is 5pm today

tell me if this bridges the gap or not

Drop the draft in right now! Paste whatever you've got for that executive summary, and let’s look at it immediately.

With a 5 PM deadline and no formal third-party data in hand, the real challenge will be reframing your appeal so HR doesn't instantly kick it back for missing required documentation. We'll want to focus on:

1. **Repositioning your role:** Tying your compensation to the national/specialized scope of your impact and internal wins rather than local cost-of-labor.
2. **Leveraging your director:** Formalizing that verbal support into an explicit managerial endorsement on business continuity and replacement cost.
3. **Structuring a bridge or deferral:** Proposing an interim freeze or conditional review so HR doesn't execute the cut before a full evaluation happens.

Paste the text, and let's tighten it up fast.

ok here's my exec summary draft

"my base pay reduction of 12% due to relocation to boise does not reflect the national scope of my responsibilities. internal project achievements and verbal director support confirm tier-level performance. i request preservation of current pay tier pending formal review."

does that do it? or does it still miss the policy requirement thing

It misses the mark for what HR needs to approve this, and as written, HR will likely reject it by 5 PM. 

Here is why:
1. **It highlights the missing requirement:** Saying *"verbal director support"* explicitly tells HR, *"I don't have written management approval or data."*
2. **It confuses performance with market rate:** *"Tier-level performance"* doesn't satisfy a geographic compensation policy. Location adjustments are about the cost of labor to replace the role, not whether you're doing good work.
3. **It leaves the data gap wide open:** If policy mandates third-party benchmark data, you cannot just skip it; you have to explain *why* standard local data doesn't apply (e.g., national specialized labor pool) and commit to the deliverable during the pause.

Here is a revised version that frames your request in HR/compensation terms and directly addresses the policy hurdle:

***

### Revised Executive Summary

> **Executive Summary**  
> This memo requests a temporary stay of the scheduled 12% geographic pay adjustment effective today, August 22, 2026, pending a formal compensation review. While standard policy references local market tiers, this role operates on a specialized, national scope with cross-regional deliverables that cannot be benchmarked against standard local labor pools. With full business endorsement from [Director’s Name/Title], we request maintaining the current compensation tier while management and HR benchmark this role against specialized national market data, to be submitted by [Date, e.g., Friday, August 29].

***

### Two critical things you need to do before 5 PM:

1. **Convert that "verbal support" into written sign-off:**  
   Send a two-line message to your director right now:  
   > *"Hey [Name], submitting my appeal for the pay tier freeze before 5 PM. Could you reply with a quick 'Approved / Supported' so HR sees management endorsement on the record?"*  
   Attach a screenshot or forward of their reply to this memo.
2. **Give HR a process out:**  
   HR rarely has the authority to wave a policy requirement permanently on the spot, but they almost always have the leeway to **pause an action** for 5–7 business days if management requests a formal evaluation.

ok the exec summary is clearly not enough on its own i get it

here's the operational continuity risk section i wrote

"im the only architect who knows the legacy integration layer. if i leave or disengage the next release slips by at least 6 weeks. replacement hire would take 90-120 days and cost 15-20% above current salary due to national specialty."

wait wait does this help? like if i frame it as a business continuity thing does that balance against the missing benchmark or am i just showing them i dont have the data

This argument helps tremendously, but the phrasing needs an adjustment because HR can interpret parts of it as an ultimatum. 

Here is how HR and People Ops read that draft:
* **"If I leave or disengage":** This reads as a threat to quit or quiet-quit. HR typically bristles at compensation appeals framed as retention ultimatums, and it gives them an excuse to dismiss the business case on tone.
* **"Replacement hire would cost 15–20% above...":** **This is actually market benchmark logic.** You are pointing out that your role recruits from a *national specialty talent pool*, not the Boise metro pool. 

Operational risk and replacement cost are the standard justifications compensation committees use to grant policy exceptions. You just need to frame it around **critical business dependency** and **cost to replace**, keeping the tone professional and objective.

Here is how to rewrite that section:

***

### Revised: Operational Continuity & Specialized Market Scope

> **Operational Impact & Critical Dependency**  
> The core responsibilities of this role oversee the legacy integration layer, for which there is currently no internal redundancy. An unmitigated disruption or transition in this position introduces an immediate risk of a 6+ week delay to [Upcoming Milestone/Release Name], directly impacting team delivery targets.
>
> **Specialized Labor Pool & Replacement Cost**  
> Because this architecture requires niche legacy systems expertise, replacement recruitment operates on a specialized national market rather than a regional labor pool. Current market lead times for this profile average 90–120 days, with replacement talent commanding an estimated 15–20% premium over current compensation levels. Adjusting compensation down to local Boise tier structures creates an artificial retention vulnerability for a critical, nationally-scoped business asset.

***

### Why this fixes the problem:
1. **It removes the personal threat:** Instead of *"if I leave,"* it frames the issue as *"introducing an unmitigated operational risk."*
2. **It addresses the data gap:** It explains *why* standard geographic tiers don't fit—because recruiting for your specific skill set requires competing nationally, where rates are higher, not locally.

does that count or is that still just words

It still just counts as words. In fact, writing *“Marcus, I support you on this”* in a quote block can backfire because it sounds like casual encouragement, not an official business endorsement. 

HR will look at that and say, *"Support you on what? Did the director review the policy? Did he approve the budget? Or was he just being nice?"*

To turn this into real leverage before 5 PM, **do not just quote him—get his paper trail.** 

Do this right now:

### Step 1: Send your director this quick message / email

> **Subject:** Quick sign-off: Relocation pay-tier review (payroll deadline 5pm)  
>  
> Hi [Director Name],  
> Following up on our conversation yesterday—I am submitting the one-page justification to HR today to keep my compensation tier based on national role scope and critical system continuity.  
>  
> Since HR requires management endorsement to pause the adjustment for review, could you reply with a quick confirmation that you support maintaining my current tier pending the formal evaluation?  
>  
> Thanks,  
> Marcus

### Step 2: How to present it in the memo

Once he replies (even a simple *"Approved, I support this"* or *"Agreed"*):

* Put a section in the memo called **"Management Endorsement"** with this language:
  > **Management Endorsement**  
  > *This appeal and the requested stay of adjustment are endorsed by [Director’s Name], [Director’s Title], citing critical operational continuity on the integration layer and national market scope for this specialized skillset. (Confirmation attached).*
* Attach a PDF or screenshot of the email thread to the back of your memo.

### What if he doesn't reply before 5 PM?

If the clock runs out and you haven't received a written reply, do **not** use the direct quote. Instead, attribute it formally to business continuity and copy him on the email submission:

> **Management Endorsement**  
> *Role scope and continuity considerations discussed and endorsed by [Director’s Name], [Director’s Title]. Management is copied on this submission for formal concurrence.*

Then, **cc your director** on the email to HR. If your director is on the thread, HR knows he's on the hook to object if he disagrees—and it puts the ball in his court to back you up.

or is that just a softer no

If you use the quote and just cc him without his actual sign-off, **HR will almost certainly execute the cut at 5 PM.** It will be a polite "no" or an automatic processing of the payroll file.

Here is the reality of how HR payroll cutoffs work:
* Payroll admins run on hard checklist logic, not nuance. If a policy requires X and Y, and an employee submits a document claiming management verbally agrees, the admin's standard operating procedure is: *apply the policy cut now; let the employee retroactively fix it later if leadership forces the issue.*
* A quote like *"Marcus, I support you"* gives HR zero authorization to stop the automated workflow.

### Your play for the next 40 minutes:

**1. Ping your director immediately on Slack/Teams (faster than email):**
> *"Hey [Name], sending the HR memo before the 5 PM cutoff. Could you reply with a quick 'Confirmed' or 'Supported' so they have written sign-off to pause the adjustment pending review?"*

**2. If you don't hear back by 4:45 PM:**
Do not use the quote. It signals to HR that you couldn't get him to write it down. Instead, send the email with your director cc'd and use this exact framing:

> **Subject:** Formal Appeal: Geographic Tier Review – Marcus [Last Name] (CC: [Director Name])
>
> HR Compensation Team,
>
> Attached is my formal appeal requesting a temporary stay on the scheduled geographic tier adjustment, supported by operational dependency and specialized national recruitment scope. 
>
> **[Director Name] is copied here in support of pausing the adjustment for the upcoming pay cycle while management completes the necessary role scope review.**
>
> Marcus

By writing *"Director is copied in support of pausing..."*, you are putting the onus on the director to speak up if he doesn't agree, and you give the HR admin cover to say, *"The director is actively on this thread asking for a pause, so I shouldn't finalize this transaction yet."*

Get that Slack out to him right now. If he replies with even one word, you have what you need.
